## 5. Discussion

The purpose of this study was to measure differences of sediment deposition across temporal and spatial scopes, focusing on ramped and scarped marsh edges. 


#### 4.1. Edge morphology: scarped vs. ramped

My results demonstrated that both of my Scarped sites had a higher median flux than two of my Ramped sites measured. However, the two Scarped sites differed in the direction of their range of minimum and maximum values of sediment deposition, as well as their geomorphology of the marsh themselves. Each Scarped marsh fit on either extreme of average elevation of the marsh profile. Considering how important elevation and relative expected inundation is to sediment transport (cite here-papers that discuss basic processes of how tide height affect how and how much sediment deposits on the marsh surface), the processes at both Scarped sites cannot be comparable. In addition, both Scarped sites are positioned at different orientations to the San Francisco Bay embayment (cite paper that is San Francisco specific, that names specific orientation in the marsh as a factor), have different protection structures around them (cite paper that talks about protected marshes vs. open marshes), and different riverine input sources to each other (Cite Thorne paper that measures distance of measured marsh points to riverine sources). Despite this, both Scarped marshes had higher median values compared to both Ramped marshes, as well as both of them had a higher range of values than the Ramped sites (Figure 28). This could allude to the natural condition that these marshes are both under-more active wave energies and decreasing sediment availability (cite paper that talks about the importance of wave energy in sediment deposition paired with less sediment available). This has been supported by the literature, as scarped marsh edge morphology is commonly demonstrative of a high wave energy environment ( @moller2002,  cite papers that talk about scarped marsh edges association with high power wind energy). For the processes of sediment deposition, this shows that the presence of a scarped edge site could mean that sediment deposition values are more extreme than at ramped marsh edge sites-and that augmentation of material closer to the marsh edge might not be as stable as further into the marsh platform (cite paper about edge effects and stability of the marsh platform). Within the Scarped edge category, Giant Marsh was exceptional amongst all four of the marshes in terms of its sediment deposition near the marsh edge. Its extreme values point to potential differences in processes that might differ from its comparative Scarped marsh edge of Corte Madera.

Ramped sites behaved similarly in terms of sediment deposition, and covered similar elevation profiles to each other. Both of these sites were nearby riverine inputs or directly adjacent to it (Buck's Landing-Gallinas Creek, San Pablo-Petaluma River), though both had different orientations to the main embayment of the San Francisco Bay as well as different protection levels. Sediment deposition near the marsh edge also proved to be dynamic in extreme values at San Pablo Marsh, but compared to further upland into the marsh platform, the values didn't exceed much higher. Throughout much of the upland marsh and throughout the seasons for the 2025/2026 sampling session, values of sediment deposition did not exceed a certain range compared with the Scarped sites. 

The Ramped versus Scarped dynamic weakened when compared between Scarped edge site Giant Marsh and Ramped edge site San Pablo Marsh, which both experienced higher values near the marsh edge but San Pablo didn't have the same extent of range of high values that Giant Marsh did. This could allude to more of a relationship between the marsh orientation and the lack of protection that both of these marshes have compared to the other two sites, pointing to the strong influence of wind waves that both of these sites are more prone to (cite additional or the same papers that talk about orientation and lack of protection as a strong effect here for sediment deposition). Wind waves have been pointed to as a strong factor influencing sediment deposition on marsh edges (cite here foundational and local papers pointing to wind waves as having a strong effect). Due to the relatively dry winter that the 2025/2026 year produced, wind could be a bigger factor in the processes at these sites, but was not able to be measured for each site due to budget and scope. Additional studies may want to consider wind as a factor to collect data from with additional marsh edge vs. sediment deposition studies.


#### 4.2 Distance from the edge vs. elevation (z*)

Distance from the edge proved statistically significant at all four sites, and within 0-6 meters from the marked marsh edge sediment deposition was highly variable in comparison to the marsh platform, which measured similar values of sediment deposition. Where this pattern differed was accounting for if sediment deposition increased or decreased with distance from the marsh edge. In Corte Madera marsh, flux as measured at its lowest compared to the marsh platform, whereas in Giant Marsh, flux was measured at its highest compared to the marsh platform. For both of the Ramped Edge sites, sediment deposition either increased closer to the marsh edge or was generally similar compared to the upland sites. This deviates from the literature, where distance from the edge was observed to increase as sediment deposition decreased (cite literature where distance from the edge of the source accounts for sediment deposition).

However, when accounting for the additional vertical parameters of the marsh, the pattern between all the marshes becomes clearer that the Scarped marsh edge sites and Ramped marsh edge sites are not inherently comparable when accounting additionally for their differences in elevation. The elevation changed the orientation of the marsh edge, as the highest elevation point measured on either transects in Corte Madera Marsh was the furthest point accounted for 24 meters from the edge of the marsh, versus the highest point in Giant Marsh measured was 2 meters from the marsh edge. Giant Marsh's extreme high values observed at this high elevation point 2 meters from the marsh edge strongly effected the LASSO analysis, which provided a larger coefficient than distance which deviates from the literature (cite Karen's paper that points to z* and distance from the edge). However, as the highest elevation site for Giant Marsh was also one of the closest to the marsh edge, it is difficult to uncouple the two effects from each other as driving sedimentation. When all sites are analyzed on their own, it is clear that distance and elevation plays a unique role within each site (Figure 29).

Distance was relatively easy to compare at each site as we had duplicates for each site. However, elevation mainly acted as a site level comparison as we had only two sites of the same marsh edge type that duplicated similar elevation ranges. Future studies should consider standardizing elevation ranges between all sites tested to observed if elevation, independent of site choice, makes a difference as a factor of sediment deposition.

Vegetation is also a factor that was measured as a site level characterization, but was not measured as a structural feature of each marsh. Vegetation, in terms of average and maximum height, percent cover, and species composition did vary between each of the sites. These vegetative characteristics as well cannot be uncoupled from the factors of elevation, as these species have specific zones of tidal inundation they can survive in and grow (cite Rankin vegetation paper). All of these marshes as well have different restoration histories that could change in which species and how each species grow throughout the marsh (cite papers specific to their restoration history-should have prompted later in the introduction more heavily in outlining each site). Additional studies should consider vegetation characteristics throughout the marsh as past studies have pointed to its relevance in sediment trapping throughout the marsh, wave attenuation, and seasonal differences in this functions throughout the marsh (cite Foster-Martinez and Moller for the attentuation and sediment settling effects of vegetation).


#### 4.3 Seasonal and Year-to-Year Patterns 

Throughout both study periods of 2022/2023 and 2025/2026, the Summer season was found to have higher flux through the bounds of May-October months. Only one site, San Pablo Marsh, was observed in the 2025/2026 season to be statistically significant in a linear model for Summer season differences in sediment deposition. Another comparison of the Summer season's role in sediment deposition at San Pablo Marsh could not be made for the 2022/2023 season at the same sampling points, as the 2022/2023 sampling started further into the unvegetated marsh than the 2025/2026.

The other Ramped marsh edge site, Buck's Landing, stood out with the highest month-to-month variation without a seasonal effect as San Pablo Marsh did. Buck's Landing geomorphically stands out between the other 3 sites, as it's closest body of water is actually the riverine source of Gallinas Creek and not the bayward embayment. The area sampled was also opposite McGinness marsh, another adjacent wetland that likely has separate processes than Buck's Landing, which is contiguous to the China Camp marsh complex. In comparison, all the remaining 3 sites sampled are opposite an the tidal influence of the San Francisco Bay Estuary, with varying protection structures nearby effecting the wave power but not influencing the input source. Past research has pointed to multiple potential sources of sediment, including riverine sources and tidal channels-one of which is directly parallel to one of the Transects tested (cite Reed, Thorne, and other papers that point to multiple sources of sediment as a source for marshes, not just the open bay). Buck's Landing sensitivity to a month-by-month basis without a seasonal inflow could indicate how sensitive this area of the marsh is to these smaller inputs from Gallinas Creek, tidal channels of China Camp, and opposite McGinnes marsh, while being largely protected from the wind waves of the San Francisco Bay that are embelmatic of summer wind waves.

Much of the extreme high and low sediment values near the Scarped sites could be sediment recirculating from the nearby mudflat instead of inputs from riverine sources and near the bay. This is further implied through other findings (cite other papers that talk about extreme sediment deposition near the marsh edge, including erosion and larger sediment deposition values), as well as the comparative dataset of Corte Madera Marsh from 2022/2023 and 2025/2026. Within the 2022/2023 year, there was a comparably higher atmospheric storm occurring during the winter, and throughout the marsh produced higher sediment deposition values than the 2025/2026 year . In addition, the distribution of values within the 2022/2023 field sampling differ with a skewness towards positive values comparative to the 2025/2026 dataset, which was comparably seasonally drier.

Past research indicates the value of atmospheric rivers and storms on sediment deposition (cite Karen paper here). Comparing the 2022/2023 and 2025/2026 datasets demonstrates this pattern as well, as overall between both marshes, specifically at Corte Madera marsh, there was overall higher deposition across the winter months especially in 2022/2023. Considering the differences in responses observed in 2025/2026 dataset between ramped and scarped marsh edges to seasonal differences, repetition at San Pablo at the same locations would assist in aiding this comparison, as during this study that comparison was not able to be made due to an offset of the transect. Comparing the direction of the distribution plot between 2022/2023 to 2025/2026 season, we see the median overall shift to the right in the 2022/2023 season. With increased comparable datapoints from San Pablo Marsh, there would be potential to see if there is a relationship of increased sedimentation during higher precipitation years across both sites measured (Figure 31). 

When considering the 2022/2023 sampling points seasonally at San Pablo that includes the unvegetated marsh points, we can see that there is a seasonal signal in the winter that differs greatly in scale compared to the main dataset (Figure 32). However, past research has pointed to this area of the marsh, closer to the bay and more frequently changing in inundation, as heavily dynamic in sediment transport (cite papers that talk about sheer stress of the bed in front of the marsh edge as a major source of sediment-I think Lacy has one of them and definitely in Foster-Martinez white paper from 2026). There is no way to tell if the sediment that was mobilized in this area further upland into the marsh, other than comparing the more upland positions sediment deposition over time, which did not appear to deviate strongly from the rest of the upland points on a seasonal scale.

There is also a tug-of-war relationship between wave action in relation to sediment deposition (cite some of the foundational papers that look into the wave action as a driver of sedimentation-including a Lacy paper). Too strong of waves, and erosion is the dominant effect, and too weak of waves, and sediment does not get mobilized far enough to reach the marshes (cite, see if this relationship is actually better). The summer season in past research specifically in the San Francisco Bay Area has pointed to wave power to be a strong factor that both mobilizes sediment from the bed form as well as moves it towards marshes (cite Lacy Seasonal Variation paper). More detailed work on how this balance of both higher sediment deposition events and increased erosion occurring specifically at Giant Marsh during the summer months balances out to keep up with sea level rise. Some past work, specifically at Whale's Tail with a similar marsh orientation and marsh edge shape, had similar findings, and conjecture was brought up that the marsh would be "cannibalizing" itself by losing area laterally, while growing area of the marsh vertically through high depositional events (cite WinklerPrins paper). Giant Marsh could be another example of this occurring in the future.



#### 4.4 Synthesis: What Control Deposition at Each Edge Type 

Variance Across Time and space was made at each of the four sites, and the finding throughout all four sites did demonstrate a pattern between edge type: Ramped sites Buck's Landing and San Pablo had their majority of their variance observed between month-to-month comparability versus Scarped sites Giant Marsh and Corte Madera had the majority of their variance observed based on the trap location within the marsh, or their distance from the marsh edge.

As scarped sites are often indicators of increased wave action, the distance from the edge of the marsh, or the trap location within the marsh, makes sense as preceding in it's effect to sediment deposition in comparison to the ramped sites. Seasonal changes in the tide rising and falling against ramped edges has more opportunity for sediment to settle out onto the edge, contrasting for the singular events of waves hitting the obstacle of a cliffed edge, creating stress against the platform (cite paper that talks about the waves interacting and undercutting the marsh edge). Considering the subtle differences within the dataset, the differences between months from the Buck's Landing and San Pablo marsh could be magnified upon closer examination to again demonstrate that within site differences would take precedence. A higher sample size is necessary to understand if indeed ramped marsh edges have a greater response to seasonal changes in sediment deposition compared to scarped marsh edges.

If this finding proves consistent with follow-on studies, it could lead to different management needs between scarped and ramped marsh edge sites. Follow-on studies should focus on specific marsh geomorphic and abiotic conditions, such as long term monitoring of the wave behavior of the site (cite paper that has long term wave interactions), suspended sediment pool (cite Ganju 2017 paper), wave direction in relation to the orientation of the marsh edge measured (not sure where to find this paper-cite here), and the unique structure of the vegetation observed throughout the marsh edge across seasonal changes (cite many papers, including Rankin, Schile, Foster-Martinez). Past literature has pointed to these specific factors being important for sediment deposition to occur, and due to the scope of this multi-comparison study (cite the Warmer Swanson paper that shows the model can take these inputs), we were not able to make these specific detailed observations that would be needed to point to specific processes of how the sediment deposition is different across these different marsh edge types. In addition, the link between erosion/progradation, or lateral movement of the marsh to the sediment loss and deposition, or vertical movement of the marsh is new and understudied (cite some of the papers that make this connection-there's one or a couple of them recently like the Echilje paper and that paper in Florida). To branch out into observing if there are process level differences at these marsh edge types, all parameters of the marsh need to be monitored in the same time scale to understand the complicated and three dimensional nature of marsh movement in order to monitor it more closely as sea level rise increases (cite some of the foundational papers that talk about the complicated, multi-faceted processes that are required to be modeled, like Fagherazzi 2020).


#### 4.5 Limitations and Future Work 

Spatially, the different site level representation of each data pointed provided an opportunity to demonstrate how different marshes could be, but on the flip side prevented accurate comparisons across marsh edge type due to differences in tidal elevations. In addition, the offset of where the Ramped marsh edge "started" between the two datasets highlights how difficult it is to dictate where the true "marsh edge" is especially with Ramped sites where there is a lack of unification on what decides the edge-the MLLW mark, or the vegetation change, or a combination of both biological and abiotic factors (site papers that have differences in where the marsh edge is dictated from). This could likely stay as a site specific decision as tidal regimes change across the world, weather patterns shift, salinity changes, etc (site specific differences in sediment deposition processes across the world, such as diurnal tidal regimes in the Gulf near Lousiana, and Indian ocean). Future publications providing criteria of how to dictate that marsh edge could aid in this field so marsh edge studies could be better standardized to understand processes and help managers as sea level rises and the very definition of a "marsh edge" could continue to change and become more dynamic with more extreme weather shifts.

Temporally, a year long dataset is not sufficient to make claims of how these marshes with different marsh edges are responsive at a seasonal level (cite papers that have critiques about single year study sites as explaining marsh processes). Past studies have considered marsh edge change based on aerial and historical imagery to observe lateral movement of the marsh edge sufficiently (cite Beagle 2015) over multiple decades. Specific to scarped marsh edges, there has been speculation that this marsh edge is part of a cycle of change that the marsh naturally goes through, eventually becoming a ramped marsh edge once equilibrium is established with sediment supply, vegetation colonization, and wind wave power (cite Fagherazzi, Beagle, and others that have postulated that there is a natural process). Considering that the two years sampled 2022/2023 and 2025/2026 differ considerably in their precipitation and wind/wave patterns, these datasets can highlight that differences occur seasonally and monthly, but cannot point to how these processes change over time without additional years sampled, as well as measurement of these abiotic forcings like wind and wave power locally measured continuously at each site. As we enter futures with expected more extreme conditions of wind, wave, and more extreme tidal fluxes from El Nino and La Nina weather processes, standardizing these comparisons to formulate a pattern will become more difficult without longer term, continuous datasets (cite Thorne paper, and the Leonardi review paper that talks about storms). This was a limitation of this study to postulate processes, and should be considered for future studies.

A major caveat of these findings is based on the smaller population size. Additional marshes of this marsh edge profile, as well as increased monitoring over longer year time sets need to be made in order to determine is this implied obversations lead to understanding processes. Past work has noted that in order to create more accurate sea level rise models, additional field collections need to be made to reciprocate these models. We need to better understand existing processes especially at the marsh edge level as sea level increases to rise and tidal changes become more extreme so we can better understand the existing condition as well as the changes ahead.

Another factor to consider between Scarped and Ramped edge marshes are their adjacency to natural habitats versus man-made structures. Both the Scarped edge sites are behind a regularly used shipping channel, Corte Madera from the Larkspur ferry terminal and Giant Marsh from the Pinole Shoals federal shipping channel (cite that Cadigan paper that talks about ferries). Both of these Scarped sites are squeezed by human infrastructure, Corte Madera with the 101 Highway and a popular shopping center and Giant Marsh with a Railroad. Both of the Ramped sites are in areas with comparably less infrastructure surrounding it, and relatively less boat traffic. The lack of human infrastructure pressures on Ramped marshes has been diagnostic of decreasing pressure on estuarine systems that are highly sensitive to wave energies (cite papers like Fagherazzi 2020 that point to the potential for upland migration as a point that is understudied and needs additional thought). The adjacency to major shipping channels to Corte Madera Marsh and Giant marsh also provide an opportunity for placement of dredged sediment, as the marshes themselves cannot expand upland as readily as the Ramped marshes can that were sampled in this study (cite studies that have talked about how thin layer placement occurred on marshes and shallow water placement). Marshes have proven to be beneficial buffers to human infrastructure in terms of storms and events of higher tidal height (cite papers that have demonstrated the benefits of coastal protection to communities). As much infrastructure and highways are built adjacent to coastal systems especially in the San Francisco Bay area, the opportunity of deciding whether to have upland migration of marshes or lateral expansion of marshes will occur not just as a protection of these important ecosystems, but in addition protection to existing infrastructure that our communities can depend on.

Scarps, and eroding shorelines can also be a signal of decreasing sediment supply arriving to the marsh (cite papers that talk about the specific balance of sediment needed in scarps). The suspended sediment pool could not be measured during this study, and that is a major limitation as we attempted to compare the sediment deposition across sites (cite Ganju 2017). Without comparing if the suspended sediment pool was the same across sites, we cannot postulate if other factors like distance from marsh edge, elevation, wind, waves, and tidal inundation levels, can fully describe conditions steering processes of sediment deposition.

This study benefited from having a quicker learning curve in the data collection so technical assistance could come from people of multiple backgrounds-some who had been advanced marine science technicians for decades as well as volunteers who had never been in a marsh before. As we encounter more circumstances where funding is scarce for long term field studies, these methods that didn't require advanced technical knowledge of sensors and technical oceanographic equipment can be scaled up quickly with relatively little training. These methods also expand opportunities for members of the public to get acquainted with marsh systems, and feel apart of the processes within them to feel a sense of ownership in protecting them. Despite needing additional technical oceanographic equipment on this project to answer broader process questions, this study served a purpose in taking a first stab at teasing apart marsh edge typology in the field in the processes of sediment deposition within the San Francisco Bay.
